lines.text: You've got the Python.
And every change to it lands as a commit.
So here are five minutes on shaping that history... searching it... and sharing it.
All familiar? Swipe on to the shell.
Our repo is a small data cleaning script, and this branch adds deduplication. Two ways to bring it in.
A merge keeps both lines, and ties them together with a commit that has two parents. The history is kept exactly as it happened.
A rebase replays your commits on top of the target. One straight line, as if the work happened in order.
So rebase this branch onto main. What happens to its commits?
Three new commits, with new IDs.
Rebase replays each change onto main. And a commit's ID covers its parent, its files, who made it and when, and its message... so every replayed commit gets a new one.
Your old commits are still in the reference log. A merge would have kept them, and added a commit with two parents.
But look at the end. Both ways finish with the very same files.
Before you push this branch, rewrite freely.
An interactive rebase lets you reorder, reword, squash, fix up, and drop commits.
Commit a fix with the fix up option, and auto squash moves it right under its target.
The fix moves up under its target, and the debug commit is dropped.
Here, four commits become two.
One rule. Never rewrite what others have already pulled.
And any rewrite of your own is undoable. The old branch is one reference log entry back.
When both sides change the same lines, or nearby ones, Git stops, and keeps three versions.
The common ancestor. Yours. And theirs.
Turn on the three way conflict style, and the file shows the ancestor as well, so you can see what each side actually changed.
Edit the file, add it, then continue. Or abort, to back out.
One trap. In a rebase, ours and theirs swap.
Ours is the branch you're rebasing onto, plus your commits replayed so far. Theirs is the commit being replayed.
Bisect is a binary search through history.
Mark one commit good, and one bad. It checks out the middle, you test it... and every answer halves the suspects.
So, a thousand commits. How many tests until you find the first bad one?
About ten.
Each test halves the suspects. A thousand commits need about ten tests, because ten halvings take about a thousand down to one.
Checking them one by one could take nearly a thousand.
That's the power of halving.
Better still... let Git run the tests for you.
Give bisect run a command, and it reads just one thing back: the exit code. That is the number every command ends with, and zero means it worked.
A good commit makes the command succeed. A bad commit makes it fail, and a failing assert counts as a failure. A special skip code tells bisect this commit can't be tested.
Anything else stops the whole run.
The best test fails only because of the bug. And keep it outside the repo, so old commits can't change it.
A pull request asks for review, and automated build and test checks, before a branch lands.
GitHub can land it three ways.
A merge commit keeps every commit. Squash makes one commit. And rebase and merge replays them as new commits in a line.
Squash suits short-lived branches.
Say you squash a three commit pull request, then add one more commit to the same branch and open a new pull request. How many commits does it list?
The next pull request shows four commits.
The squash commit isn't made of your three commits... so Git still sees them as unmerged. They come back, along with the new one. The three old ones are only duplicates.
And here, they even conflict.
After a squash merge, start a fresh branch from main.
Branch length is the risk.
In trunk-based development, everyone merges into one trunk, at least daily, through short-lived branches that exist for review and checks.
Bigger changes still land in small steps, with feature flags and branch by abstraction.
A long-lived branch drifts. The gap grows every day, so the longer it lives, the bigger the final merge... and keeping it in step means resolving the same conflicts again.
So... eight things to keep.
Merging keeps both parents. Rebasing replays your commits, with new IDs. Rewrite only what you haven't pushed.
A conflict has a base, ours, and theirs. Bisect finds a bug in about ten tests, and bisect run reads the exit code.
A pull request can land by merge, squash or rebase, and after a squash, retire the branch. And keep your branches short.
Next up... the shell, where those exit codes come from.
